references.text: Laying hands on the head of the sacrificial animal is a central act in the burnt offering, showing identification between the offerer and the sacrifice.
In the peace offering, one also lays a hand on the animal's head before slaughter, the same ritual action as in the sin offering.
The priest lays his hand on the bull's head for a sin offering for himself; this same ritual pattern is repeated here.
Laying hands and slaughtering at the same place as the burnt offering is also mentioned regarding a sin offering of a male goat for a leader.
A parallel text about a sin offering of a female goat for an ordinary person, with the same ritual of laying on of hands and slaughter.
The place for slaughtering the burnt offering on the north side of the altar is the same place where the sin offering must be slaughtered.
On the Day of Atonement, Aaron lays both hands on the goat's head and confesses the people's sins, showing the transfer of sin to the sacrificial animal.
The Epistle to the Hebrews explains that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, highlighting the necessity of slaughter in the sin offering.
